To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

recovery of fecal chromium was greatest when fecal samples were frozen fresh and then thawed and digested with concentrated HNO3, but was not improved by the double ashing or by the weaker acid digestion.
the use of frozen fecal samples for chromium analysis in cattle is superior to the use of feces that are dried in a forced draft oven or in a microwave.
Cr recovery from feces was greater from fresh feces than dried feces, and that Cr recovery was greater from feces digested with concentrated rather than weak nitric acid.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a method of recovering Cr from fecal and ruminal samples.
the use of Cr as a digestibility indicator in cattle.
the recovery of fecal chromium (Cr) used as a digestible marker in ruminants.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of frozen fecal samples, thawed before analysis, and a nitric acid wet digestion procedure is the preferred method for the analysis of feces to determine the recovery of Cr.

Cr recovery from feces was greater from samples that were frozen fresh and thawed before digestion than from either forced draft or microwave oven-dried feces, and that recovery of Cr from dried fecal samples was improved when a wetting agent, such as Tween 80, was included in the nitric acid digestion.
Cr can be used in fecal digestibility trials with cattle, but it is essential that fecal samples be frozen fresh, then thawed, and digested with concentrated HNO3 in the presence of a wetting agent.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Cr recoveries from fresh feces were greater than from dried samples and that recoveries were greater from feces digested in nitric acid than from samples digested with the double ashing method.
recovery of Cr from fresh fecal samples that are later thawed is greater than that from fecal samples that have been dried.
recovery of Cr from fresh feces is superior to recovery of Cr from oven-dried feces.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Cr recoveries are improved when Cr-mordanted feces are frozen fresh and then thawed prior to digestion with concentrated nitric acids.
Cr recoveries are higher when Cr is extracted from feces that were frozen fresh than when they are dried prior to Cr extraction, and this is particularly true when concentrated nitric acid is used.
fecal chromium used to estimate digestibility of feedstuffs can be recovered by digesting fecal material that is frozen fresh and later defrosted with concentrated nitric or sulfuric acid.
